hlni.insight: The same aggregate (100%) can represent entirely different component distributions.
hlni.audienceGap: Students assume degree titles imply a specific, uniform experience.
hlni.viewerChange: Replaces label-based comparison with a component-based assessment method.
hlni.support: Arithmetic logic: different subsets can sum to identical totals.
hlni.payoff: The viewer now knows to ask for specific assessment breakdowns rather than choosing by degree name alone.

shots.name: The Identical Boxes
shots.visual: Two identical boxes appear on screen. Both are labeled '100% Degree'.
shots.dialogue: Think B.Com and BBA are just different names for the same thing?

shots.name: The Deconstruction
shots.visual: Boxes split. Box A shows 40% independent research/60% lab work. Box B shows 40% team projects/60% theory.
shots.dialogue: Look at the breakdown. A 100% total can hide completely different daily realities.
shots.cameraPerformance: Fast-paced animation showing the bars splitting into percentage segments.

shots.name: The Next Question
shots.visual: A student looking at a course document, pointing to the assessment section.
shots.dialogue: Stop comparing labels. Ask: What is the specific breakdown of assessment types for this semester?

creativeSummary.keyCreativeIdea: Use an aggregate counterexample to show that degree names are insufficient for comparison; assessing the component mix is necessary.

selected.title: The Total Value Trap
selected.audienceGap: Assuming that the same degree title implies the same mix of experiences.
selected.hlni: The same total can result from different component values; an aggregate alone cannot tell you the underlying mix.
selected.viewerChange: Understands that high-level aggregates (like total credits or degree name) mask significantly different components.
selected.concept: Visualizing two identical '100% Course' bars that reveal completely different, non-overlapping component lists.
selected.device: Animated bar charts that 'deconstruct' into different sub-components.
selected.support: The claim follows from the displayed arithmetic, not an invented university metric.
methodSteps: Show two clearly illustrative component lists with the same total.
Ask for the breakdown before drawing a conclusion from the total.
selected.interpretationRule: Use the breakdown to ask what differs; do not infer identical experiences from equal totals.
selected.visibleProof: An explicitly illustrative arithmetic counterexample makes the hidden difference visible.
selected.payoff: Use the breakdown to ask what differs; do not infer identical experiences from equal totals.
selected.limitations: Keep figures clearly illustrative and do not assign them to actual programmes, credits or outcomes.

comparedWith.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
comparedWith.device: Split-screen view of two worksheets where the student fills in columns for 'Work Product,' 'Criterion,' and 'Available Feedback.'

comparedWith.hlni: A short illustrative activity can reveal where you need help or what you want to investigate next; it cannot determine which degree suits you.

conceptSelection.contrast: The selected mechanisms provide distinct ways to handle uncertainty: 'Trust' focuses on auditing workload (Assessment Audit), 'Connection' focuses on identifying personal research gaps (Task Journaling), and 'Discovery' focuses on mathematically demonstrating why labels are often misleading (Aggregate Counterexample).
